Anthony Wayne. Nicknamed "Mad Anthony" for his fearlessness and aggressive tactics, he was one of the Continental Army's most daring combat leaders.

Wayne rose from militia officer to major general through sheer combat talent and ferocity, serving under George Washington with distinction throughout the war. He commanded the Pennsylvania Line and earned his nickname for his willingness to undertake dangerous missions and fight against overwhelming odds with unshakeable determination.

His most famous action was the midnight bayonet assault on Stony Point in July of 1779, a virtually impregnable British redoubt on the Hudson River. He captured it with minimal casualties through audacious tactics that became a textbook example of nocturnal assault.

Wayne endured the horrors of Valley Forge alongside Washington and his troops, sharing their suffering and emerging as a beloved figure to the enlisted men. He fought in numerous engagements from the Brandywine campaign through the southern theater, accumulating a reputation for never refusing a dangerous order and always fighting to the last.

After the war, he led expeditions against Native Americans on the American frontier, most notably defeating a confederacy of tribes at Fallen Timbers in 1794 to secure Ohio.
